What happened? Why did it suddenly speed up?

The man regulating the brakes did let it go too quickly, and subsequently was not able to stop it at all.
Is that fire friction from the metal on metal? What does it burn? Maybe the coating?

It's definitely heat from the friction of chain. The quick flame ups towards the end may be the break pads igniting.

I don't really know much about the inner workings of this mechanism. Perhaps some old navy dog will stop by with some answers.

The smoke at the beginning is crusty silt and sand stuck to the chain from previous moorings, the fire is likely from the friction brake. I think it happened because the anchorman was over-compensating, opening it too much and once it caught speed he wasn't able to close it down again.

You can read more about mooring equipment here: http://www.ijinmarine.net/apps/blog/all-equipment-used-when-mooring
That makes a lot of sense. In the video it looks like the guy panics and starts spinning as far as he can the opposite direction.

This isn't that uncommon. The friction brake on anchor chains need to hold A LOT of force. Very hard for the operator to judge as the anchor chain often piles on top of itself inside the cable locker so it doesn't pay out uniformly. It doesn't take much to build up too much momentum to stop.

I've seen two brake failures. In one the anchor was being prepped for anchorage while still underway. The anchor was swept back into the hull causing significant damage but allowed the brake to catch. The second one was stationary. It ran out to the bitter end in deep water, but the anchor shackle held. The bow dropped almost 20ft before recovering (5000 TN ship). Sick feeling in my stomach as the whole hull shuddered and the bottom dropped out of the world for a couple seconds. The bounce back was enough to tie a knot in the anchor chain. It took us 3hrs to figure out how to untie it - that shit ain't in the manual.

Those guys should have cleared the fo'c'sle long before they did. The amount of force involved is terrifying. If something jams, there's easily enough force to tear the windlass out of the deck or turn it into shrapnel.
